#### The round trip — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Whether "the two directions are inverses" is a property of the duality or of the aggregate — by running the round trip on a sum and on a max.

`capture(key, agg)` emits each record with `before` taken *before* the update, so every record is (old → new). `foldBack` then recovers the table from either log, because every record names the result.

`recoverEvents` is the conditional direction. On the sum log it returns [5, 3, 2, 6, 8] — exactly the events. On the max log it returns [5, 0, 0, 1, 2], and `ambiguity` counts **36** event sequences consistent with that same log.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-duality-memory/ch06-duality-memory.svg" alt="The round trip — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — every changelog record carries the OLD value</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-duality-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: every changelog record carries the OLD value" width="980">

`before` is captured BEFORE `acc` is updated, so the record is (5 → 8). That `before` is what makes the log invertible and what lets a summing consumer retract. Drop it and the record says only "8", which is a final state rather than a change.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — folding back works for ANY aggregate — each record names the result</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-duality-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: folding back works for ANY aggregate — each record names the result" width="980">

`cur` just takes `r.new` each time, so it ends at 8 for the max log and 24 for the sum log. Changelog → table always works, because every record states the result. It is the other direction that is conditional.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — differencing recovers the events — for the SUM</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-duality-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: differencing recovers the events — for the SUM" width="980">

`out` reaches [5, 3, 2, 6, 8], which is exactly key "a"'s event values [5, 3, 2, 6, 8]. The subtraction inverts the addition, so nothing was lost in aggregating. This is the round trip the duality is usually described by.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the SAME function on the max log loses 2 events</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-duality-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the SAME function on the max log loses 2 events" width="980">

When `r.new == r.old` the record tells you nothing about the event that caused it — any value from 0 to 5 produces the same record, so `n` multiplies by 6. `howMany` = 36: that many event sequences give this identical changelog. `maxBack` = [5, 0, 0, 1, 2] is not the events and no amount of care makes it so.

</details>
